title: At the café: ordering without pointing
goal: Order food and drinks in full sentences, and learn the accusative case — the ending a noun takes as soon as it becomes the target of an action.
bekal: order with Я хочу … and Я буду …
put feminine nouns into the accusative
know when masculine nouns do NOT change
name the most common Russian foods and drinks
ask for the check and thank the server

dialogs.title: Диалог — The first lunch
dialogs.intro: Ani and Марко walk into the campus café. Watch the noun endings after хочу and буду: the feminine ones change, the masculine inanimate ones don't.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Yes. I'll have borscht and black tea.
lines.literal: yes. I — will — borscht — and — black — tea.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I'd like a pizza and water, please.
lines.literal: I — want — pizza (accusative) — and — water (accusative), please.

lines.speaker: Официант:
lines.literal: water — with — gas — or — without — gas?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: No, thank you. Just the check, when you can.
lines.literal: no, thank-you. only — check, when — possible.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Ice cream in winter? You're already Russian.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Everyone here eats ice cream in winter. I'm just learning.
lines.literal: here — all — eat — ice-cream — in-winter. I — simply — learn.

notes: **The accusative is the ending for the target of an action.** In *Я хочу пиццу*, the pizza is what's wanted — it's the target, not the doer. Feminine nouns in **-а/-я** change to **-у/-ю**: пицц**а** → пицц**у**, вод**а** → вод**у**, книг**а** → книг**у**. ⚠️ This is the ending beginners forget most, because in English "pizza" stays the same whether it's the subject or the object.

**Masculine inanimate nouns do NOT change in the accusative.** *Я хочу борщ* — борщ stays борщ. *Я читаю журнал* — журнал stays журнал. Big good news: half the objects you'll use need nothing done to them at all.
**Neuter nouns don't change either.** *Я хочу мороженое* — exactly the same as the dictionary form. So of the four noun types, only **one** changes in the accusative singular: the feminine.

**Я буду … is the most typically Russian way to order.** Literally "I will be" — the future of быть, with no other verb. Russians use it exactly the way English speakers say "I'll have …". *Я буду кофе.* — I'll have a coffee. Completely natural, and it sounds softer than *Я хочу*.

**Я хочу is a little more direct, but not rude.** ⚠️ Unlike English, where *I want* sounds pushy in a restaurant, Russian *Я хочу* is perfectly normal — as long as you finish with пожалуйста. What really feels rude is just naming the dish without a sentence.

**С means "with", без means "without", and both change the noun's ending.** *с газ**ом*** (sparkling, instrumental), *без газ**а*** (still, genitive). For now learn this pair as chunks — two phrases you'll use every time you order water in Russia.

**Счёт means the check, and asking for it has its own etiquette.** The standard phrases: *Счёт, пожалуйста* or *Можно счёт?*. ⚠️ In Russia the server usually does **not** bring the check before you ask, because that would feel like showing guests the door — so don't sit waiting for it.

grammars.title: Accusative singular — only one row changes
body: Compare the second column with the first. Only the feminine rows are different.
after: ⚠️ The second row is the only place at A1 where "alive or not" matters. Masculine nouns for living beings take the genitive ending **-а** when they're the object: *Я знаю Иван**а***, *Я вижу брат**а***, *Я люблю кот**а***.

The verbs whose objects go into the accusative are the most common action verbs: **хотеть** (to want), **есть** (to eat), **пить** (to drink), **читать** (to read), **смотреть** (to watch), **знать** (to know), **любить** (to love), **покупать** (to buy), **делать** (to do).

grammars.title: Хотеть — a verb that obeys no group
body: Its first half follows Group I, its second half Group II. Learn it whole; you'll use it every day.
after: After хотеть you can have a noun (*Я хочу чай*) or a verb in its dictionary form (*Я хочу есть* — I'm hungry, literally "I want to eat"). *Я хочу пить* means "I'm thirsty".

blocks.title: Three things about eating in Russia that surprise newcomers
items: **Soup is eaten every day, not now and then.** A full Russian lunch has a fixed order: первое (first course, always soup), второе (second course, meat or fish with potatoes or porridge), and компот or чай. Turning down soup in a Russian home can feel odd.

**Tea is drunk hot and endlessly, but almost always without milk.** Russians drink чай with sugar, lemon or jam — not with milk. ⚠️ Order *чай с молоком* and you'll get it, but you'll be taken for a Brit.

**Rice isn't a staple.** Russia has картошка (potatoes), хлеб (dark bread) and гречка (buckwheat). Rice exists, but as a side dish, not the center of the plate. Learners from rice-eating cultures who hunt for rice at every meal will go hungry fast — or quickly learn to love dark bread.

exercises.prompt: Put into the accusative. Remember: only the feminine changes.
Fill in the right form of хотеть.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: пиццу — борщ — воду — мороженое — курицу — чай
хочу — хочешь — хочет — хотим — хотите — хотят
Я буду борщ. — Счёт, пожалуйста. — Я хочу воду без газа. — Что вы посоветуете? — Очень вкусно.
Я буду чёрный чай. — Я хочу пиццу, пожалуйста. — Вода без газа. — Что вы посоветуете? — Очень вкусно! — Счёт, пожалуйста.
